summary: A restatement of the Network Working Group's documentation conventions, updating RFC 3 on how notes in the series should be written and shared. It was itself replaced by RFC 16 and was updated by later notes in the same series (RFC 24, RFC 27 and RFC 30).

plainLanguage.summary: This is the updated rulebook for how to write and share notes in the group, replacing the first set of rules.

questions: what was the network working group
subtitle: The rules for writing and sharing Network Working Group notes: write anything, keep it timely, and send it around.

tldr.problem: Early network researchers needed a way to share ideas about HOST software without people treating every written statement as authoritative or holding back unpolished thoughts.
tldr.mechanism: Notes may be produced by anybody at any site, may contain any thought related to the network, need a serial number, author, date and title, and are mailed in one copy to a list of nine people.
tldr.outcome: This revision of RFC 3 was itself replaced by RFC 16 and updated by RFC 24, RFC 27 and RFC 30.

today: RFC 10 is obsoleted by RFC 16 and was updated by RFC 24, RFC 27 and RFC 30. It obsoletes RFC 3.

sections.title: The Network Working Group
sections.content:
This note, dated 29 July 1969 and written by S. Crocker at UCLA, is a revision of NWG/RFC #3. It lists the group's members at the time: Steve Carr at Utah, Elmer Shapiro and Bill English at SRI, Steve Crocker at UCLA, John Haefner at RAND, and Paul Rovner and Jim Curry at Lincoln Labs. Membership is not closed.

The Network Working Group (NWG) is concerned with the HOST software, the strategies for using the network, and initial experience with the network. Its work is documented through notes that may be produced at any site by anybody.
sections.plainLanguage: A small group of people is building something new together, and they write notes to each other to keep track of ideas.

sections.title: What a Note May Contain
sections.content:
The content of a note may be any thought or suggestion related to the HOST software or other aspect of the network. Notes are encouraged to be timely rather than polished. Philosophical positions without examples, suggestions without background, and questions without attempted answers are all acceptable. The minimum length is one sentence.

The RFC gives two reasons for being so relaxed. First, people tend to treat anything written down as authoritative, and the group wants to encourage discussion of less than authoritative ideas. Second, people hesitate to publish something unpolished, and the group hopes to ease that.
sections.plainLanguage: You are allowed to share half-baked ideas, even a single sentence, because the point is to talk, not to be perfect.

sections.title: Form of a Note
sections.content: Every note should carry four things: the words Network Working Group followed by Request for Comments: and a serial number; the author and affiliation; the date; and a title. The title need not be unique. Serial numbers are assigned by Steve Crocker at UCLA.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note gets a number, a name tag for the writer, a date and a title, like labeling a drawing.

sections.title: Distribution and Addresses
sections.content:
One copy only is sent from the author's site to each of nine people, starting with Steve Crocker at UCLA and ending with Jerry Cole at SDC; the list also includes Bob Kahn at BB&N and Larry Roberts at ARPA. Reproduction, if desired, may be handled locally.

The rest of the note gives the current postal addresses and telephone numbers of those people and asks readers to correct them as necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: You mail one copy to each person on the list, and if someone wants more copies they can make them at home.
